topics.title: Paging, Multi-Level Page Tables & The TLB
topics.summary: Translating virtual addresses to physical frames with hardware cache acceleration.
topics.plainWords: Think of a Library Catalog and Secret Agent P.O. Boxes: Every student (process) is given an identical notebook numbered pages 1 to 1,000 (virtual addresses). But in reality, the books are stored across 10 random warehouses in different cities (physical RAM frames). The library index desk is the Page Table. The Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) is a sticky note on the librarian's desk with the 16 most recently looked-up book locations: if your book is on the sticky note (TLB hit), you get it in 1 second; if not (TLB miss), the librarian must walk into the back archive to read the multi-level card index.
topics.keyTakeaway: Remember that TLB misses can be handled either in hardware (x86 MMU walking page tables) or in software (MIPS/RISC-V OS trap). A Page Fault is fundamentally different from a TLB miss: a TLB miss is a quick hardware cache miss, while a page fault requires disk I/O to swap a missing page into RAM.

infoNeeded.title: Virtual to Physical Address Translation Steps
points: Virtual Address Decomposition: Split into Virtual Page Number (VPN) and Page Offset based on page size (e.g., 12-bit offset for 4KB pages).
TLB Lookup: MMU inspects TLB associative cache using the VPN. On a hit, physical frame number (PFN) is concatenated with the offset immediately.
Page Table Walk: On a TLB miss, the MMU or OS walks the multi-level page table using CR3/page directory pointers.
Page Fault Handling: If the Present/Valid bit in the page table entry (PTE) is 0, a page fault exception triggers the OS kernel to fetch the page from swap disk.
